lawyer:
Amirul Islam with A Baset Mazumder, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Md Joynal Abedin, Advocate ------ For the Respondents 2 & 3.
parties:
Meghna Vegetable Oil Industries Ltd ------ Petitioner
vs.
Bangladesh Oil, Gas and Mineral Corporation (Petro Bangla) and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment: 4. Mr Islam argues that when a petitioner obtained the gas line it did not take it like an individual citizen but as an industrial establishment  for production of commodities for consumption by  the nation and, as such, the High Court Division  should exercise its power of judicial review under  Article 102 in respect of the order impugned. He  continues to argue that the petitioner's fundamental  right to do business as contemplated under Article  40 has been infringed as the petitioner owns the  business which can not be run without enjoyment of  gas. Therefore, according to him, disconnection of supply of gas by removal of meter is infringement   of such right. He also argues with reference to Article 15 of our Constitution that both Principles of Fundamental state policy and Fundamental Rights  should be taken into consideration in deciding the  state policy and as in this case the petitioner entered  in joint venture with a foreign country for doing its business it does so on the basis of state policy and   the gas belonging to the State the impugned order violative of Article 15 of our Constitution. This contention is untenable for firstly, the petitioner did  not enter into any agreement for supply of gas with  the Government nor with the Government owned   company. The agreement of supply of gas is with the respondent 2, a limited company. Secondly, on facts of this case the impugned action is relatable to the contractual rights and obligations between the  two private contracting parties ie the two  incorporated companies. The decision cited by Mr. Islam from Indian jurisdiction in the case of Mahabir   Auto Stores and others vs. Indian Oil Corporation. AIR 1990 (SC) 1031 can hardly support himboth for the distinguishable facts of the cases of the Indian Jurisdiction and that of ours and for the wording of Articles 226 and 32 of the Constitution. of India and Article 102 of ours. In Mahabir the appellant entered into contract with Indian Oil   Company for supply of Lubricant. The Supreme   Court with reference to Article 14 of the Indian   Constitution held that every action of the state   executive authority is subject to rule of law and must be informed by reason and Article 14 would be applicable to such exercise of power. In the instant   case there was no such contract for supply of gas by the state executive. Thus, the decision does not help   Mr. Islam. The decision in 45 DLR 33 also does not   help Mr Islam in the facts of this case. Rather the decision in the case the National Engineer Ltd vs.  Director Military Land & Cantonment etc. 12 BLD 563 = 44 DLR 144 applies to this case wherein after review of a number of cases it has been  observed, "we are also of the view if there is a breach' of any terms of agreement for sale as contained in Annexure-D, the remedy lies in a properly constituted suit for damage against the party to such  contract for breach of any term." In the similar way   the Supreme Court of India in the case of Radha  Krishna Agarwal vs. State of Bihar, 1977 (SC) 1496  negatived the contention that when the state or its official purport to operate within the contractual field  the grievance of the citizen could be remedied by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution. In the instant case before us the gas line was disconnected on the unpaid bill which the petitioner states to be false and the disconnection is in terms of the agreement (Annexure-C). Thus when for breach of a term and a condition of an agreement an action is taken by a party the remedy lies in a properly constituted suit and not in writ jurisdiction this case another strong ground for failure of this petition is that it raises a disputed question of fact as   to the gas bill which, according to the petitioner, is I false. Thus, we do not find any substance in the contentions of Mr Islam and the petition does not merit issuance of a Rule.
